items.title: ‘Completely Unscorched!’: Kathy Ireland Praises God After Husband’s Miracle Survival, Reveals Bible Survived Fire
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Former supermodel and businesswoman Kathy Ireland is praising God for her husband Greg’s survival after the engine of his commercial […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Former supermodel and businesswoman Kathy Ireland is praising God for her husband Greg’s survival after the engine of his commercial fishing boat caught fire and he miraculously survived.

Ireland revealed on Instagram that the boat was entirely destroyed, with one item notably surviving the harrowing ordeal: a Bible.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Kathy Ireland® (@kathyireland)

“Greg went to the harbor to assess the damage,” she wrote. “The boat and all its contents are no more. Besides our commercial fishing licenses, the only thing on the boat that survived is his Bible! Completely unscorched! My heart is overflowing full!”

Ireland shared remarkable images of the torched vessel and the totally pristine Bible, sparking awe from friends and fans.

In an earlier post, she initially described the difficult nature of losing the fishing boat.

“Life is really hard and really beautiful,” Ireland wrote in an Instagram description of a video showing the boat on fire. “God is great. I’m on the road for business and grandchildren so Greg was out alone. Engine exploded and a fire quickly melted all navigation equipment and survival raft!”

The Kathy Ireland Worldwide founder went on to thank those who prayed and helped rescue Greg. Beyond all else, though, Ireland praised the Lord even amid so much loss.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Kathy Ireland® (@kathyireland)

“Most of all, we thank our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ for this miracle of his survival,” she said.

Ireland concluded her message with the text of Isaiah‬ ‭43‬:‭2‬, which reads, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; And through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched, Nor will the flame burn you.”

Continue praying for Ireland and her family as they cope with the fallout of this tragedy.

items.title: Senator Intensely Questions Cissie Graham Lynch on LGBT Views During Confirmation Hearing
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Important.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine (D) intensely questioned Cissie Graham Lynch, the granddaughter of the late Rev. Billy Graham, on LGBT issues during her Senate confirmation hearing to serve as ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom.

Listen to the latest episode of the “Quick Start” podcast

Kaine asked Lynch, who supports a biblical understanding of marriage as a lifelong union between one male and one female, how she would work as ambassador “to protect … LGBTQ folks from persecution.” Lynch immediately responded that, in her official capacity, she would have a “responsibility to protect people of all faiths” and does not believe “anyone should ever be criminalized or persecuted for their personal beliefs.”

The senator, who identifies as Catholic, told Lynch there are “countries around the world [that] criminalize just being gay, being LGBTQ” — an interesting line of inquiry for a politician who has been intensely supportive of celebrating Islam, stating in the past that Muslim Americans “enrich the fabric of our communities,” given the religion is deeply opposed to homosexuality.

Kaine pressed Lynch to explain her view, which she expressed in February 2021, that certain LGBT nondiscrimination laws could jeopardize Christian religious freedoms, a concept that apparently was difficult for the Virginia lawmaker to understand. For context, Lynch — who has worked alongside her father, Franklin Graham, at the humanitarian organization Samaritan’s Purse — wrote in a 2021 opinion article for Fox News that the “extreme” Equality Act would “erode” religious liberties for Christians.

If enacted into law, the Equality Act, which has been introduced in Congress numerous times but has never passed through the Senate, would amend existing civil rights laws in the U.S. to explicitly prohibit any form of discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity across areas like employment, housing, and education. Lynch, for her part, has argued such legislation would override religious liberty protections, barring faith-based organizations that hold to a biblical view of sexuality from operating according to their deeply held religious convictions.

During her Senate hearing this week, Lynch specifically mentioned to Kaine the case of baker Jack Phillips, a small business owner in Denver, Colorado, who skyrocketed to national news in 2012, when he declined to make a custom wedding cake for a same-sex couple. He has faced numerous lawsuits in the years since for similar issues, all of which he has won to date.

Nevertheless, Lynch argued Phillips is a prime example of an American who has faced intense attacks because of his personally held religious beliefs when it comes to marriage. She also mentioned he has never turned away customers due to their sexual practices or personal ideologies, noting Phillips “for years” has “served people of the LGBT community” without issue.

Listen to the latest episode of the “Radical Revelations” podcast

While the ambassador-at-large nominee has her own views of sexuality and marriage, she told the senators in Congress she has always sought to engage in dialogue about these issues “with kindness” and “with respect.”

“I’ve talked about on my platform many issues that are divisive in our culture and we are in a culture that teaches us that, if we believe something differently, that we can’t get along with somebody, that that’s hate speech,” she said.

On a global scale, Lynch said she “would never be able to support something [such as a Ugandan law] where it’s criminalizing people … for their sexual identity, for their sexual preference.” She reaffirmed to Kaine she is committed, if confirmed, to “represent[ing] people of all faiths,” and drew particular attention to the religious persecution happening around the world: “People are dying. People are being persecuted. People are put into jail. There’s 80 countries with blasphemy laws.”

“I’ve learned that through my years of working when I work in the countries with people I often don’t have the same beliefs, but we come together,” she said of her humanitarian work with Samaritan’s Purse, adding her goal is to “find that common ground to help people on a bipartisan mission.”

Before a vote on Lynch’s confirmation can reach the full Senate, she must first be approved by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where Republicans currently hold a 12-10 majority. In the full Senate, Republicans outnumber Democrats at 53-47.

items.title: Anthony Ippolito Bet on Himself to Play Young Sylvester Stallone. It’s One of the Best Performances of the Year.
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: By the time anyone in Hollywood wanted Sylvester Stallone’s boxing script, he and his wife, Sasha, were down to their last $106. Producers Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler saw it as a star vehicle for someone like Burt Reynolds or Robert Redford, and they offered the unknown writer $75,000 fo
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

By the time anyone in Hollywood wanted Sylvester Stallone’s boxing script, he and his wife, Sasha, were down to their last $106. Producers Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler saw it as a star vehicle for someone like Burt Reynolds or Robert Redford, and they offered the unknown writer $75,000 for it, according to TCM. When he refused, the offer went to $100,000, then $150,000. Stallone’s condition never moved. He would sell Rocky only if he got to play Rocky.

Nearly 50 years later, Anthony Ippolito made his own version of that bet. “No one asked me to audition for this,” he told RELEVANT. “I just heard the project was getting made and really wanted to get into the conversation.” He sees some of himself in Stallone’s story, and he expects other people will too. “Hopefully a lot of people in creative fields feel that way once they see the film and see what he went through.”

It paid off. In I Play Rocky, Peter Farrelly’s film about how Rocky got made, Ippolito gives a stunning performance as a young Stallone, broke and stubborn and still years from fame, and the movie around him is every bit as good. It opened in select theaters Nov. 6 and expands nationwide Nov. 20.

“It’s very tempting in a position like that to go in the other direction and just say thanks for the money,” Ippolito says of Stallone’s choice. “But it’s not what he decided to do. We wouldn’t be sitting here talking about him fifty years later if he went the other way with it.” He calls the money Stallone turned down “a remarkable amount” and the choice “very, very tough.”

The film covers roughly 1972 to 1976: the broke New York years, the drive west, the script Stallone wrote after watching underdog Chuck Wepner go 15 rounds with Muhammad Ali, the standoff over who would star in it and a shoot that nearly came apart. It ends before the world knew who Sylvester Stallone was.

“He’s known for what he became, as a big star,” Ippolito says. “This movie’s about something entirely different. Just stripping all that away and focusing on what he was like before that.”

To prepare, Ippolito spent a long stretch hunting down footage of Stallone from the early ’70s. “It was tough because he wasn’t a big name at this time,” he says. “But I tried to find whatever I could.”

He also talked with Stallone over Zoom. “It’s incredibly informative, what he was willing to share with me, and I just appreciated his vulnerability,” Ippolito says. “I know it’s not easy to talk about some of this stuff in one’s life. He was in a pretty dark period of time before Rocky got made. So just telling me some of the little details about what that period of time was like was huge.”

Watch our conversation with Ippolito on The RELEVANT Podcast:

In the film, Stallone is living close to the edge, working low-paying jobs between auditions, with a father, played by Matt Dillon, who doesn’t think much of his son’s ambitions. AnnaSophia Robb plays Sasha, who pushes him to use his real name and to start writing. Later, the film follows the shoot itself: a punishing schedule, a director, John G. Avildsen (Jay Duplass), who wants most scenes done in a single take, and producers scrambling to cover a budget shortfall.

Then there was the boxing, which Ippolito had never done. “I had to figure out how to do that,” he says. “It was tricky, but we figured it out.” The work came in small pieces: learning to hit a speed bag, going over fight choreography with Stephan James, who plays Carl Weathers, and building the rest “piece by piece.” Between the fights and the famous training montage, Ippolito says the montage was harder. “We were doing a lot of that stuff in December in Philly, and it was pretty cold,” he says. “The whole crew was kind of battling the elements. Neither was a walk in the park.”

Critics have mostly come away impressed. On Rotten Tomatoes, the film holds an 86 percent score, and the site’s critics consensus singles out Ippolito’s “uncanny embodiment” of Stallone. Variety’s Owen Gleiberman wrote that the film understands how the underdog story on screen echoed the one it took to get Rocky made in the first place.

United Artists finally agreed to let Stallone star, but on a budget of about $1 million, and only after Chartoff and Winkler put up a completion bond to cover any overruns, according to TCM. Stallone took the standard writer’s fee and $20,000 to play the part. “As far as I was concerned, if I didn’t get this part it was the only shot I would ever get,” Stallone said later. “I was willing to do it for nothing.”

“When people saw the original Rocky, they walked out feeling empowered and hopeful, and hopefully they had a fun time in the theater,” Ippolito says. “It’s pretty similar with this one. That’s the goal.”

Rocky won Best Picture. The writer who wouldn’t sell it without himself attached was nominated for best actor and best original screenplay.

items.title: In the Age of AI, the Non‑Sacramental Life Is Not Worth Living
items.author: Fr. Brian K. Carpenter, STD
items.summary:
Fr. Brian K. Carpenter, STD

AI has the potential to disrupt the Christian mimetic chain, which requires an encounter with a model capable of interiority, volition, and relationship.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Fr. Brian K. Carpenter, STD

René Girard’s mimetic theory posits that desire is not intrinsic to each individual but is mediated through others. Girard believes that people choose mediators, or “models” whom they desire to be, and conform their desires to those of the selected model. The result is that the human person is formed within a network of imitative behavior and desire that is personal, relational, and incarnational. While this can and often does lead to rivalries among human beings, when properly ordered, mimetic desire leads the human person to more fully actualize the imago Dei. This ultimately occurs through the imitation of Jesus Christ, who is God incarnate. But for most people, imitation of Christ is mediated by a model who has already successfully learned to imitate Christ. Hence, St. Paul gives the instruction, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Cor 11:1). This Christian mimetic chain, as I call it, is essential to human formation as well as the formation of Christian disciples. 

Christianity is not learned by reading the Scriptures but is lived incarnationally. It is a “way of life” that requires an active participation mediated through an encounter with individuals who already embody it. These individuals are the people Girard would call “mediators” or “models” of desire. Girard holds that mimetic desire is rooted in interiority, volition, and relationality. As such, a suitable model of imitation will have the ability to examine an interior life, exercise free will, and form relationships that lead all parties towards their proper telos (“intended destiny”) of union with God. While the saints fit this description, for most people, the Christian mimetic chain is forged in a more proximate space. Family members, teachers, pastors, and friends become the models who form our desires. 

This Christian mimetic chain is threatened in the age of artificial intelligence. AI is rapidly invading the spaces where human formation occurs, such as education, communication, social platforms, and even religious education. While aspects of this technology are promising, AI poses a real risk to human formation as it increasingly governs the distribution of “models” to be imitated, and therefore, the formation of human desire. This has the potential to disrupt the Christian mimetic chain, which requires an encounter with a model who is capable of interiority, volition, and relationship. 

AI faces limitations in all three areas. AI cannot desire, it can merely optimize. It does not willfully choose “the good”; it simply predicts. It does not inhabit a world of meaning and relationship; instead, it processes correlations. In short, AI is simply a simulated model (in the Girardian sense). It is never an authentic mediator of desire.

Yet it cannot be denied that AI is entering into the very spaces where both human and Christian formation occurs. Rather than encountering other human beings, these spaces are being filled with “intelligent” machines. Studies show that AI has increasingly become “a personalized source of guidance, emotional support, and decision-making.” Here, we must begin to inquire about the impact and potential dangers of non-human models on the Christian mimetic chain.

The Christian tradition deepens Girard’s thoughts by providing a clearer vision of human anthropology and our telos. The Christian belief that all people are made in the imago Dei contains a corollary truth best summed up by St. Augustine, who wrote, “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you” (Confessions 1.1). This is the notion that being made in the imago Dei has a built-in telos: union with God. To fully actualize the imago Dei in such a way that leads to union with God requires more than an imitation of God; it requires an actual participation in the life of Christ.

With this in mind, I contend that AI’s threat to disrupt human and Christian formation highlights the necessity of the sacramental life of the Church. This is because the sacramental life of the Church is the means for human beings to participate in the life of Christ. The sacramental life is never lived in a manner that isolates the individual and Christ from all others. Rather the interiority of the sacramental life requires the believer to engage willfully with Christian community in an embodied way so as to actualize the relationship between the individual believer and Christ. In other words, an individual can only become fully actualized as a human being (a creature made in the imago Dei) by willfully choosing to participate in the life of God. Such participation in the divine life is only possible through the sacraments. Jesus himself affirmed this when he stated, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you” (John 6:53).
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

All human formation, and Christian formation in particular, is ordered towards assisting human beings to become more fully actualized. The fully actualized human being is the one who is fully conformed to the imago Dei in which all human beings are made—namely, Jesus Christ. For all other human beings, to become fully actualized requires not simply imitation of Christ, as Girard contends, but participation in the actual life of Christ. This is something that AI cannot provide, despite all its promises. Participation in this life requires the sacraments, which in turn requires an embodied encounter with an “other” human being who can model the interiority, volition, and relationship required by the sacramental life. This is a task that AI cannot and never will be able to accomplish. At best, AI could help a person learn about the sacramental life and its necessity for human beings to become fully actualized. But it will never provide the means for human beings to become fully actualized. That can only occur through encounter and participation in the sacramental life. Anything else will be at best a simulacrum of a human being fully alive. Thus, Socrates’s famous insight regarding the “unexamined life” might be updated for the digital age: “The non-sacramental life is not worth living.”

*A fuller, scholarly development of this argument is currently under review in an academic theological journal.
